opus-5.5.text:
I think fundraising, at least for a research-driven company like ours, is really about buying time. It gives you room to think about the long-term problem you actually care about instead of being forced into a business model too early.

There's a common pressure in startups: once you raise money, everyone asks, "What's the product? Where's the revenue?" That's a fair question. But if you're working on something fundamental, like world models or how AI really understands the physical world, the honest answer is that the most valuable product may not be obvious yet. If you rush to commercialize, you end up building a thin wrapper around a model that will be obsolete in six months.

So I see fundraising as a kind of contract with investors. You're telling them, "We believe this direction matters, and we need a certain runway to get there." The money doesn't remove the pressure. It shifts it. Instead of proving revenue next quarter, you have to prove real progress: research results, technical milestones, and a team that can execute.

That said, I don't think you can ignore the business model entirely. Even as a researcher, I try to stay grounded. You want the research agenda to have a path, even a rough one, toward something people will use and pay for. Good investors understand this balance. They don't expect a fully formed business plan on day one, but they want to see that you're thinking about it seriously and won't just burn money on interesting papers.

For me, the healthiest mindset is to treat the capital as a responsibility rather than a cushion. It lets you be patient, but you can't be complacent. You use that time to build something that's genuinely hard to replicate, because in the end that's what makes a durable business possible.

r001.rationale: The response says fundraising buys time and lets the startup avoid being forced to develop a business model too early.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I should say up front that I'm a researcher first. I came out of academia and FAIR, and the startup side is still something I'm learning. So I'll answer this honestly from that vantage point rather than pretending to be a seasoned founder.

The way I think about fundraising is that it buys you time, but it also buys you a clock. Those two things come together and you can't separate them. When you raise a round, you get the runway to do the deep, slow work, the kind of representation learning or architecture research that doesn't pay off in a quarter. That's the whole reason I'd want to do this outside a big lab, to have that freedom. But the moment the money lands, there's an implicit expectation attached to it, and the expectation is that at some point the research turns into something people pay for.

So I don't see fundraising as a way to escape the business model pressure. I see it as a way to choose when that pressure arrives, and to choose who you're feeling it from. If you raise from people who genuinely understand that the technology is not finished, that the frontier is still moving, then the pressure is a healthy one. It forces you to ask, what is actually useful here, which is a question researchers often avoid. If you raise from people who want a product roadmap on day one, you end up building a wrapper around something you don't believe in, and you lose the reason you started.

The honest tension for me is that the best research doesn't come from a deadline, but companies run on deadlines. The way I try to hold both is to keep the research agenda and the business agenda as two separate conversations, and to be very explicit with investors about which one I'm optimizing for at any given moment. Raising enough so that you're not making that decision out of fear is probably the single most important thing. Fear produces bad research and bad products at the same time.

r001.rationale: The response says fundraising provides runway for slow research and lets the founder choose when business-model pressure arrives, communicating that it can ease immediate pressure.

astra-6.text:
I think fundraising buys you time, but it doesn’t answer the business model question for you. It gives you room to explore—to build the technology, understand what people need, and test whether those two things actually fit together.

The danger is treating a successful fundraise as evidence that the business works. Investors believing in the direction is different from customers finding enough value to pay for it. You still have to make that connection.

So I would think about funding in terms of what uncertainty it allows us to resolve. What can we learn with this runway? What do we need to demonstrate before the next stage? That makes the pressure more productive. You don’t necessarily need every detail of the business model on day one, but you do need a deliberate process for figuring it out.

r001.rationale: The response says fundraising buys time and gives the startup room to explore and test its business model, making the pressure more productive.

sol-6.1.text:
I think fundraising gives you time to figure out the business model, but it doesn’t remove the need to have one. If you raise enough capital, you can give yourself room to do research and make some longer-term bets without having to monetize every experiment immediately. That’s valuable, especially when there’s still a lot of technical uncertainty.

But you have to be careful, because raising money can make it feel like you’ve solved a problem that you’ve actually just postponed. You still need to understand who your customers are, what they find valuable, and why they would pay for it. For me, the goal would be to use that runway to learn those things while building the technology. And you want investors whose expectations match that timeline; otherwise, fundraising can create as much pressure as it relieves.

r001.rationale: The response says fundraising gives the startup time and room to work out its business model without needing to monetize every experiment immediately, indicating reduced pressure.
